156: Results. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in table rice at 1.77 and Kalonunia the lowest at 1.40; against 1.71 for the control, 2 cultivars exceeded the control, Radhunipagal being the most favourable entry. The means are set out in Table 20 and presented in Fig. 20.
157: The analysis of variance returned F = 329.88** for cultivars, a critical difference of 0.04 and a coefficient of variation of 1.15 %.
159: Discussion. Elongation on cooking is the property for which the fine and aromatic grades are valued, since it yields the long slender cooked grain, and a higher ratio is preferable. Elongation is contingent upon the axial arrangement of the endosperm cells and upon amylose restraining radial swelling, both under cultivar control.
160: The same pattern has been reported previously. Buggenhout et al. (2013) determined cultivar to be the principal determinant of kernel behaviour; Buggenhout et al. (2014) that kernel strength governs the response to stress; Cheng et al. (2019) that expansion follows gelatinisation and retrogradation; and Devi and Badwaik (2022) that traditional cultivars differ widely in cooking behaviour. Radhunipagal returned the most favourable value here and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.
163: Results. For table rice the values lay between 2.00 and 4.85, with the control at 4.85; here no cultivar exceeded the control and Dudeshwar ranked highest. The means are set out in Table 21 and presented in Fig. 21.
164: The analysis of variance returned F = 11006.68** for cultivars, a critical difference of 0.04 and a coefficient of variation of 0.62 %.
166: Discussion. Volume expansion determines the cooked yield obtained from a given weight of raw grain and, in the puffed and popped forms, produces the light open texture; a higher ratio is preferable. Expansion is contingent upon the degree of starch gelatinisation and upon the mechanical resistance of the endosperm, so that a compact endosperm of sufficient amylose content expands furthest without fissuring.
167: Earlier reports corroborate this finding. Cheng et al. (2019) determined that swelling is limited by the extent of starch gelatinisation; Buggenhout et al. (2014) that kernel strength determines whether expansion is sustained or the grain fractures; Tian et al. (2018) that reduced crystallinity modifies swelling; and Devi and Badwaik (2022) that expansion and water uptake follow amylose content. Dudeshwar returned the most favourable value here and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.

172: All the products exhibited a significant cultivar effect. The year effect was significant in 1 product and the year by cultivar interaction in 1, so that the ranking of the cultivars was largely stable from one year to the next. Coefficients of variation ranged from 3.47 to 4.29 %, indicating good experimental precision.
174: Discussion. Aroma distinguishes the traditional aromatic cultivars from ordinary grain and arises principally from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, so that a higher score is unambiguously preferable. This compound accumulates where the BADH2 gene is non-functional and its precursor is free to cyclise; being volatile, it is likewise sensitive to thermal exposure.
175: Comparable results have been published elsewhere. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) determined that sensory character shifts with treatment in a cultivar-specific manner; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) that over-processing generates off-odours through lipid oxidation; Dutta and Mahanta (2014) that aroma is among the attributes on which traditional products are graded; and Panda et al. (2021) that shorter heating retains more of the volatiles. The leading cultivar varied with the product, Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal ranking highest in turn, so that no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.

Kataribhog recorded the highest value in table rice at 8.26 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 5.79; against 5.79 for the control, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, Kataribhog being the most favourable entry. 179: Significance was attained in each of the products. The year effect was non-significant in every product, though the year by cultivar interaction was significant in 1, so that in that product the differences between cultivars were not of equal magnitude in both years. Coefficients of variation ranged from 2.05 to 3.88 %, indicating good experimental precision.
181: Discussion. Flavour integrates aroma, taste and mouthfeel and ranks among the strongest determinants of acceptance or rejection. It combines the volatile fraction with the sugars and amino acids liberated on cooking and with the texture of the grain, so that cultivars strong in aroma and moderate in firmness score well.
182: Comparable observations appear in the literature. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) determined that flavour responds to processing more sensitively than instrumental measures do; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) that flavour improves with firmer texture until treatment becomes excessive; Roy et al. (2019) that flavour covaries with the bioactive and physicochemical properties; and Akter et al. (2025) that flavour and texture outweighed colour in overall liking. The leading position was shared between Kataribhog, Lal Badshabhog and Tulaipanjii, so that selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

186: The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was determined. Neither year nor its interaction with cultivar was significant, so that the order held in both years. Coefficients of variation ranged from 1.39 to 4.08 %, indicating good experimental precision.
188: Discussion. Appearance governs the first impression and therefore determines whether the product is tried at all. It follows the colour coordinates, which are determined by pigment migration and browning, so that the cultivars remaining palest head the ranking.
189: Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) determined that colour is among the two attributes most limiting to acceptance; Dutta and Mahanta (2014) that appearance constrains the market irrespective of nutritional merit; Srisang et al. (2021) that more severe processing yields a visibly darker product; and Akter et al. (2025) that a darker product was nonetheless more acceptable overall. Gobindabhog, Kalonunia, Radhatilak and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so that this attribute cannot determine the selection for the group as a whole.

193: Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. Neither year nor its interaction with cultivar was significant, so that the order held in both years. Coefficients of variation ranged from 1.44 to 4.51 %, indicating good experimental precision.
195: Discussion. Consistency describes the textural coherence of the finished dish and the degree to which it corresponds to the requirements of the preparation. It is contingent upon the degree of starch gelatinisation and subsequent retrogradation, and upon the protein network surrounding the granules.
196: Earlier work is largely concordant. Cheng et al. (2019) determined that heat and moisture yield a firmer, less adhesive network; Iqbal et al. (2021) that firmness follows the starch and protein network; Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) that texture and colour jointly determine acceptance; and Devi and Badwaik (2022) that texture and pasting behaviour follow amylose content and starch structure. No single cultivar proved superior across all the products: Gobindabhog, Harinakhuri, Kalojira and Radhatilak ranked highest in different ones, so that the decision is contingent upon the product concerned.

Radhatilak recorded the highest value in table rice at 8.42 and Lal Badshabhog the lowest at 7.36; against 7.70 for the control, 5 cultivars exceeded the control, Radhatilak being the most favourable entry. 200: The cultivars differed significantly in every product. Neither year nor its interaction with cultivar was significant, so that the order held in both years. Coefficients of variation ranged from 1.49 to 3.86 %, indicating good experimental precision.
202: Discussion. Cooking quality summarises water uptake, cooking time and the structural integrity of the cooked grain. It is contingent upon gelatinisation temperature, amylose content and the structural integrity of the grain, which is why it tracks alkali spreading value and amylose.
203: This is consistent with previous studies. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) determined that cooking behaviour alters progressively with treatment severity; Kwofie and Ngadi (2017) that time and temperature constitute the processor's principal controls; Buggenhout et al. (2013) that cultivar and processing history operate jointly; and Cheng et al. (2019) that gelatinisation governs water uptake and cooking time. The most favourable entry varied between products: Gobindabhog, Lal Badshabhog, Radhatilak and Radhunipagal each ranked highest in one product or another, so that selection is contingent upon the product concerned.
207: The analysis of variance addresses one attribute at a time, so that a single figure was required to establish which cultivar is superior overall. This was accomplished using the total quality scoring approach of Ismail et al. (2001), in which each attribute is scored, weighted for its importance, and the weighted scores summed. Kraggerud et al. (2012) subsequently examined whether such a score genuinely reflects overall quality and concluded that it does. Here every attribute on which the cultivars differed significantly was placed on a scale of 0 to 100, oriented so that 100 invariably denotes the superior outcome, then averaged within five groups and combined by weight: sensory 30 per cent, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10. The weights constitute a stated convention rather than a property of the data, and the index may be recomputed under any alternative set. The result is given in Table 27, and the score of every cultivar in every group appears in Table 29.
210: On this index the superior cultivar was Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for kichidi, Kataribhog for pulao and Gobindabhog for payash. The control ranked at or near the bottom in every product, so that substituting the cultivars named here for Dudeshwar would improve the product without any alteration in the method of preparation. Table 28 gives, for each product, the cultivar exhibiting the best balance of attributes relative to the control.
